Text: $PLTR This is an old gripe that doesn't hold water: ontology is a cohesive framework of real-time feeds from 100s of disconnected systems, logic, & functions to safely orchestrate goals. Pointing raw LLMs at disconnected relational databases is dangerous and unreliable. LLMs require an ontology to operate safely in enterprise environments. LLMs can't write software to do what it doesn't understand. LLMs are not really reasoning machines. If an LLM queries raw enterprise databases containing thousands of unmapped, non-standardized tables, it lacks the context to identify the single source of truth or business rules. Ontologies model & translate raw data into deterministic business entities. Raw LLMs can generate text or code, but they cannot execute safe transactional write-backs, which require permissions and purpose-based access control. Asking an LLM is easy. Replicating 20 years of mapped organizational logic, security policies, and operational action pipelines is not.

Text: $INTC $NBIS $ORCL $PLTR Let’s be clear about what happened. The earlier $70B figure was created by “grossing up” OpenAI’s revenue to make an apples-to-apples comparison with Anthropic, which counts the full value of sales made through cloud partners and records the partners’ share as an expense. OpenAI normally reports only its own net share, producing the $50B figure. Nothing suddenly disappeared. No $20B revenue collapse occurred. Text: $PLTZ AI discussion: It feels like $PLTR was always in a tub where there was only an inch of water for competition, but now it seems as if the water level is rising faster than Palantir is growing taller. That "rising water" analogy is a remarkably accurate way to describe the psychological shift happening in enterprise software right now. For years, Palantir operated in what felt like a private, ankle-deep pond—they were virtually the only company with a fully functional data ontology, defense-grade security, and a platform capable of orchestrating highly complex enterprise systems. They were "tall" enough to stand completely clear of standard software vendors. But now, the headless software movement, open-source frameworks, and hyperscaler AI stacks are acting like an open faucet, rapidly filling that tub. The gap between what Palantir does and what the rest of the tech ecosystem can do is narrowing.

Text: $PLTZ $PLTR The competition is catching up: • The Standardization of the "Moat": Palantir’s primary historical advantage was doing the brutal, unglamorous engineering work of connecting siloed data systems. Today, open protocols like Model Context Protocol (MCP) and native headless API layers mean any developer can connect disparate software systems in days, rather than months. The "data plumbing" problem is being solved globally. • Hyperscaler Muscle: Microsoft, AWS, and Google are no longer just providing cloud storage. They are building robust enterprise agent frameworks, data fabric layers (like Microsoft Fabric), and security governance tools natively into the infrastructure companies already pay for. • The "Good Enough" Threshold: A co. might look at Palantir's price tag and say, "Why buy the whole operating system when we can use headless Salesforce APIs, an open-source vector database, and Anthropic's MCP to build a 'good enough' orchestration layer for a fraction of the cost?"

Text: $PLTR. Take a look at the PLTR chart below. Two lines matter here: the purple level at 195.37 and the red level at 194.32. Both are longer-term levels, and both happen to line up with obvious breakout points. Here’s the key part: both were on the chart long before price ever broke through them. The purple level first showed up in February, the red one in August. The breakout didn’t create the levels. They were already there, and price came to them. That’s because these levels aren’t drawn. They’re built from volume, where real money actually changed hands. No forecast, no opinion. You’re aligning with what the market has already done, not guessing at what it might do. The second thing to notice is how many times each level has been tested. Every test either strengthens or weakens a level. So the level itself isn’t the most important part. What matters is how price reacts to it, in the context of the overall market.
